o: CSF reduces the effective weight of the brain from 1500 g to 50 g
The arachnoid is CSF-proof but needs dural support. (Last's p. 558)
Dura and arachnoid are blended along the whole cranial base
Last's: the only place they blend is the aqueduct of the cochlea. (Last's p. 559)
Vessels and nerves pierce dura and arachnoid at the same place
They never run between the two membranes. (Last's p. 559)
The spinal arachnoid strands form a complete posterior median septum
It is incomplete. (Last's p. 559)
The lateral part of the cisterna magna contains the vertebral artery and PICA
It receives CSF from the foramen of Magendie. (Last's p. 559)
The pontine cistern receives CSF from the foramen of Magendie
It receives it from the lateral foramina of Luschka. (Last's p. 559)
The interpeduncular cistern contains the third and fourth cranial nerves
Also the basilar terminal branches and pituitary stalk. (Last's p. 560)
The chiasmatic cistern lies below the optic chiasma
It lies above the chiasma, beneath the rostrum, and contains the anterior communicating artery. (Last's p. 560)
Last's says the outer dural layer is never invaginated by any cranial nerve
It is ordinary periosteum and is not prolonged into the spinal dura. (Last's p. 560)
The dural folds chiefly prevent forward–backward mass displacement of the brain
They minimize rotary displacement; concussion results more readily from rotation. (Last's p. 560)
The free margin of the tentorium lies at a higher level than its attached margin
It contains no venous sinus. (Last's p. 560)
The third and fourth nerves pierce the roof of the cavernous sinus lateral to the dural ridge
They pierce the triangular roof medial to the ridge from the free tentorial margin. (Last's p. 560)
The falx cerebri projects into the foramen caecum like a peg
Last's calls it an enlarged Sharpey's fibre. (Last's p. 561)
The falx cerebelli contains the inferior sagittal sinus
It contains the small occipital sinus; the inferior sagittal is in the free border of the falx cerebri. (Last's p. 561)
Dividing the falx at autopsy lets the tentorium fall
The falx suspends the tentorium. (Last's p. 561)
The superior sagittal sinus begins at the crista galli
It begins a short distance above the foramen caecum. (Last's p. 561-2)
The accessory meningeal artery supplies dura over the cavernous sinus
It enters through the foramen ovale. (Last's p. 562)
The middle meningeal artery passes in front of the auriculotemporal nerve
It passes between its two roots. (Last's p. 562)
Near the pterion the middle meningeal artery often lies in a bony tunnel for a centimetre or more
The frontal branch then lies over the precentral gyrus. (Last's p. 562)
Haemorrhage from the posterior branch is said to cause contralateral motor weakness
Last's says it may cause contralateral deafness (superior temporal gyrus). (Last's p. 562)

questions.s: Concerning the meningeal vessels and diploic veins (Last's):
o: The middle meningeal veins, not the artery, groove the skull
They lie between the artery and bone. (Last's p. 562)
Most middle meningeal veins leave through the foramen spinosum
Most join the sphenoparietal sinus; some leave via the foramina spinosum and ovale. (Last's p. 562)
There are two parietal diploic veins on each side
One frontal, two parietal and one occipital. (Last's p. 562)
The pterion lies 3 cm above the midpoint of the zygomatic arch and in front of the frontozygomatic suture
It lies behind and above the frontozygomatic suture. (Last's p. 562)

questions.s: Concerning the nerve supply of the dura (Last's):
o: Most of the supratentorial dura is supplied by the ophthalmic nerve
Via the tentorial nerves. (Last's p. 562)
The anterior part of the middle fossa is supplied by the mandibular nerve
The anterior part is the maxillary (middle meningeal nerve); the posterior part the mandibular. (Last's p. 563)
The under surface of the tentorium is supplied by IX and X
The dura around the foramen magnum is C1–3. (Last's p. 563)
The upper surface of the tentorium is supplied by the vagus
It is supplied by the tentorial branches of the ophthalmic nerve. (Last's p. 562-3)
The inferior sagittal and straight sinuses receive no blood from bone
They lie in the inner layer folds, not between the two layers. (Last's p. 563)
The superior sagittal sinus drains the frontal pole
It does not; superior cerebral veins enter it obliquely against the flow. (Last's p. 563)
The straight sinus usually turns into the left transverse sinus
The superior sagittal usually turns right. (Last's p. 563)
The surface marking of the transverse sinus is higher than the superior nuchal line
Last's says it is lower than commonly thought, along the superior nuchal line. (Last's p. 563)

questions.s: Concerning the sinuses of the posterior fossa (Last's):
o: The jugular bulb occupies the posterior and largest compartment of the jugular foramen
(Last's p. 564)
The superior petrosal sinus enters the sigmoid sinus at its lower end
It enters at the upper end; the occipital sinus enters the lower end. (Last's p. 564)
The occipital sinus drains the choroid plexus of the fourth ventricle
It communicates with the internal vertebral plexus at the foramen magnum. (Last's p. 564)
Veins accompany the vertebral arteries within the skull
No veins accompany the vertebral or basilar arteries. (Last's p. 564)
Each cavernous sinus holds about 1.5 ml
It is spindle-shaped in lateral view. (Last's p. 566)
The floor of the cavernous sinus is the body of the sphenoid
The floor is a narrow strip of endosteum on the base of the greater wing; the medial wall is the body. (Last's p. 564)
The anterior wall of the cavernous sinus plugs the medial end of the superior orbital fissure
It is largely taken up by the ophthalmic veins. (Last's p. 565)
The sphenoidal air sinus tends to shrink posteriorly with age
It tends to increase posteriorly with advancing years. (Last's p. 566)
The internal carotid artery pierces the roof just medial to the anterior clinoid process
It enters the back of the sinus from the foramen lacerum. (Last's p. 566)
Within the cavernous sinus VI lies medial to the internal carotid artery
It lies lateral to the artery, then below it. (Last's p. 567)
No nerve lies lateral to V or medial to VI in the cavernous sinus
III slopes down crossing medial to IV and V. (Last's p. 567)
The mandibular division lies in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus
Strictly it does not contact the lateral wall. (Last's p. 567)
The inferior petrosal sinus drains most of the cavernous sinus blood
It leaves beneath the petroclinoid ligament. (Last's p. 567)
The inferior petrosal sinus enters the jugular foramen lateral to IX
It enters the anterior compartment medial to IX. (Last's p. 567)
The superior petrosal sinus receives veins from the internal ear
Through separate foramina in the petrous bone. (Last's p. 567)
The inferior ophthalmic vein drains entirely into the cavernous sinus
Much of its blood drains through the inferior orbital fissure to the pterygoid plexus. (Last's p. 567)
The inferior petrosal sinus is the first (highest) tributary of the internal jugular vein
It joins a short distance below the skull base. (Last's p. 568)
The foramen of Vesalius lies lateral to the foramen ovale
It lies medial to the foramen ovale. (Last's p. 568)
The "danger area" of the face lies above the level of the deep facial vein
Between the angular and deep facial routes to the sinus. (Last's p. 568)
Last's says the ophthalmoplegia of cavernous sinus thrombosis is the usual cause of death
Ophthalmoplegia is not dangerous; retrograde thrombosis of the inferior petrosal sinus and medullary veins is usually fatal. (Last's p. 568)
Extradural haemorrhage most often arises from the frontal branch of the middle meningeal artery
It may compress the motor area and cause contralateral hemiparesis. (Last's p. 568)
Subdural haemorrhage contaminates the CSF
Only subarachnoid haemorrhage does. (Last's p. 568)
Last's says no intracranial haemorrhage ever separates the two dural layers
Nor the pia from the brain. (Last's p. 568)
Subdural haemorrhage usually comes from a ruptured middle meningeal vein
It usually comes from a superior cerebral vein entering the superior sagittal sinus. (Last's p. 568)
Up to 20 olfactory filaments on each side pierce the dura over the cribriform plate
They cross the subarachnoid space to the bulb. (Last's p. 568)
A patent vein through the foramen caecum is present in most adults
It is present in only 1%. (Last's p. 568)
The anterior ethmoidal nerve leaves the fossa through a slit beside the front of the crista galli
It enters near the back of the cribriform plate. (Last's p. 568)
The anterior ethmoidal nerve has a long course in the anterior cranial fossa
Its course there is very short. (Last's p. 568)
Pars distalis cells are 50% chromophobes, 35% acidophils and 15% basophils
The pars distalis is 75% of the gland. (Last's p. 569)
Acidophils secrete ACTH
Acidophils secrete GH and prolactin; basophils ACTH, TSH, FSH, LH. (Last's p. 569)
Neurosecretory material travels down the pituitary stalk at about 3 mm/day
Bound to neurophysin. (Last's p. 569)
Vasopressin comes mainly from the paraventricular nucleus
Mainly from the supraoptic; oxytocin mainly from the paraventricular. (Last's p. 569)

questions.s: Concerning the pituitary and its relations (Last's):
o: The pars intermedia probably secretes MSH
It consists of colloid-filled vesicles behind a cleft. (Last's p. 569)
The function of the pars tuberalis cells is known to be gonadotrophin secretion
Their function is not known. (Last's p. 569)
There is no blood–brain barrier in the posterior pituitary or median eminence
(Last's p. 570)
In the transsphenoidal approach via the septum the nasal cavity is entered
The nasal mucosa is elevated and the septum removed; the nasal cavity itself is not entered. (Last's p. 570)
A rising pituitary tumour presses on the lower anterior part of the chiasma
Causing temporal field loss. (Last's p. 569)
In the optic canal the ophthalmic artery lies above and medial to the optic nerve
The artery comes from below and lateral; the nerve from above and medial. (Last's p. 570)
The intracranial optic nerve is clad only in pia
It gets its dura and arachnoid at the optic canal. (Last's p. 570)
The intracranial optic nerve is supplied by the ophthalmic artery
Branches of the anterior cerebral artery from the chiasma supply it. (Last's p. 570)
III runs just below and parallel to the posterior communicating artery
Pupillary fibres are on its outer part. (Last's p. 570)
The pupillary fibres of III stay dorsal along the whole intracranial course
They lie dorsal, then medial, then inferior as the nerve enters the sinus. (Last's p. 570)
IV runs lateral to III in the interpeduncular cistern
Just below the free tentorial margin. (Last's p. 570)
IV curls around the peduncle above the posterior cerebral artery
It curls below the posterior cerebral and above the superior cerebellar artery. (Last's p. 570)
The trigeminal nerve leaves a groove about 5 mm wide on the petrous border
It passes beneath the superior petrosal sinus there. (Last's p. 570)
The whole trigeminal ganglion lies within Meckel's cave
Only the posterior half does; the anterior half lies in front of it. (Last's p. 570)
The greater petrosal nerve lies beneath the trigeminal cave
Between the two layers of dura. (Last's p. 570)
The trigeminal cave opens forwards into the middle fossa
It lies in the middle fossa but opens backwards into the posterior fossa. (Last's p. 571)
Much of the trigeminal ganglion blood supply comes via the accessory meningeal artery
It runs up along the mandibular division. (Last's p. 571)
The dura around the trigeminal ganglion is supplied by the ophthalmic nerve
It is supplied by the nervus spinosus (mandibular). (Last's p. 571)
Transient facial palsy after an extradural middle fossa approach is attributed to traction on the greater petrosal nerve
Oedema at the geniculate ganglion. (Last's p. 571)
The motor root joins the mandibular division before the foramen ovale
They join in the foramen ovale. (Last's p. 571)

questions.s: Concerning nerves in the posterior fossa (Last's):
o: The trigeminal motor root emerges above and medial to the sensory root
It spirals to enter Meckel's cave below it. (Last's p. 571)
In Meckel's cave the ophthalmic fibres lie most laterally
The mandibular lie most laterally, ophthalmic most medially. (Last's p. 571)
VI pierces the clival dura some distance above its brainstem origin
Then runs up between the dural layers. (Last's p. 571)
Last's says the lesser petrosal nerve always leaves through the foramen ovale
It leaves through the foramen ovale or the petrosal foramen. (Last's p. 571)
The facial nerve pierces the front of the upper part of the fundus
The cochlear nerve pierces the front of the lower part. (Last's p. 572)
The labyrinthine artery usually arises from AICA
It is usually a branch of the basilar, but often arises from AICA. (Last's p. 572)
The foramen singulare transmits the nerve to the posterior semicircular duct
It lies behind the vestibular area. (Last's p. 572)
The vestibular nerve pierces the fundus anteriorly
It pierces it posteriorly, by upper and lower divisions. (Last's p. 572)

questions.s: Concerning the petrous bone in the posterior fossa (Last's):
o: In the neonate the subarcuate fossa is as large as the internal acoustic meatus
It lodges the flocculus. (Last's p. 572)
The subarcuate fossa lies medial to the internal acoustic meatus
It lies lateral, below the arcuate eminence. (Last's p. 572)
The endolymphatic sac lies beneath the inner layer of dura
It hangs from the aqueduct of the vestibule. (Last's p. 572)
VI is resistant to raised intracranial pressure because of its short intracranial course
Its long intracranial course makes it vulnerable; lateral rectus palsy is often early. (Last's p. 572)
The spinal accessory rootlets come from the upper five or six cervical segments
They emerge behind the denticulate ligament. (Last's p. 572)
The spinal root of XI ascends medial to the vertebral artery
It passes over the denticulate ligament lateral to the artery. (Last's p. 572)
IX and the inferior petrosal sinus share the anterior compartment
X and XI lie in the middle compartment. (Last's p. 572)
In the jugular foramen XI descends medial to the vagus
It descends lateral to the vagus; IX and XI lie lateral to X. (Last's p. 572-3)
Perilymph drains to the subarachnoid space through the aqueduct of the cochlea
It opens in the notch indented by IX. (Last's p. 572)
The hypoglossal rootlets unite into a single root before entering the canal
They form two roots separated by a dural septum that may ossify. (Last's p. 573)
The hypoglossal canal lies in the junction of basiocciput and jugular process
(Last's p. 573)
The vertebral artery gives its meningeal branches after piercing the dura
It gives them before piercing the spinal dura. (Last's p. 573)
Last's calls PICA perhaps the most tortuous artery in the body
Its coils lie between the XII, XI and X rootlets. (Last's p. 573)
The basilar artery produces the median groove of the pons
It does not; it is usually curved to one side. (Last's p. 573)
The vertebral artery runs between the lowest XII rootlets and the highest C1 rootlets
In front of the denticulate ligament. (Last's p. 573)
The vertebral arteries unite at the upper border of the pons
They unite at the lower border; the basilar ends at the upper border. (Last's p. 573)
The internal vertebral plexus acts as a bypass of the diaphragm
During sudden rises in abdominal pressure. (Last's p. 574)
The internal vertebral veins contain valves
There are none, so cancer may spread from breast, prostate, thyroid and kidney. (Last's p. 574)
The spinal dura is firmly attached to the posterior longitudinal ligament on the axis body
Elsewhere it lies free. (Last's p. 574)
Epidural and extradural spaces are different spaces
The terms are synonymous. (Last's p. 574)
The lowest denticulation of the denticulate ligament lies at the L1 root
(Last's p. 575)
The filum terminale is part of the cauda equina
The cauda equina consists of nerve roots only. (Last's p. 575)
The spinal subarachnoid space holds about 75 ml of CSF
Half of the total 150 ml. (Last's p. 575)
The denticulate teeth attach to the dura opposite the issuing nerve roots
They attach between the issuing roots. (Last's p. 575)
Cranium strictly means the skull without the mandible

Strictly the skull includes the mandible.
Cranium is often used for the brain-containing part. (Last's p. 643)
The most striking feature of the upper surface is its symmetry

Last's: its asymmetry; one side is set in front of the other.
This is reflected in the hemispheres and lateral ventricles. (Last's p. 643-4)
The parietal foramen transmits an emissary vein from the superior sagittal sinus
It lies alongside the tortuous part of the sagittal suture. (Last's p. 644)
The lambda lies at the posterior pole of the skull

It lies above the posterior pole.
It is where the sagittal and lambdoid sutures meet. (Last's p. 644)
An interparietal bone is not an accessory bone

It is a separate entity when the cartilaginous and membranous occipital parts fail to fuse.
Sutural (Wormian) bones are accessory. (Last's p. 644)
The external occipital protuberance lies about 6 cm above the lambda
It lies about 6 cm (2.5 inches) below the lambda. (Last's p. 644)
The superior nuchal line marks the internal attachment of the tentorium
It lies at the junction of neck and scalp. (Last's p. 644)
Sternocleidomastoid is attached to the medial third of the superior nuchal line

Trapezius takes the medial third; sternocleidomastoid the lateral two-thirds.
Splenius capitis inserts into the lateral third deep to it. (Last's p. 644)
The highest nuchal line gives origin to occipitalis and the galea
Beneath it bare bone covers the occipital pole. (Last's p. 644)
The coronal suture is straight above and tortuous below the inferior temporal line
It is tortuous above and straight below the inferior temporal line. (Last's p. 644)
The asterion is where the parietomastoid, occipitomastoid and lambdoid sutures meet
It is the meeting place of the temporal, parietal and occipital sutures. (Last's p. 645)
The pterion is a single point where four bones meet
Last's: it is not a single point but an area with an H-shaped pattern of sutures. (Last's p. 644-5)

questions.s: Concerning the temporal fossa and mastoid (Last's):
o: The lateral mastoid surface is built from a downgrowth of the squamous part
Incomplete fusion leaves the squamomastoid suture. (Last's p. 645)
The temporalis fascia is attached only to the inferior temporal line
It is attached to the superior line and the polished strip between the lines. (Last's p. 645)
The infratemporal crest is level with the upper border of the zygomatic arch
It marks the lower limit of the temporal surface of the greater wing. (Last's p. 646)
The coronoid process lies under cover of the frontozygomatic suture
It lies under cover of the temporozygomatic suture. (Last's p. 646)
Last's says the term "zygoma" should not be used
It can mean either the arch or the zygomatic bone. (Last's p. 646)
The posterior pillar of the arch is grooved by the anterior fibres of temporalis
It is grooved by the posterior fibres, which glide across it. (Last's p. 646)
A vertical groove above the external meatus lodges deep superficial temporal vessels
It lies on the squamous bone. (Last's p. 646)
The zygomatic bone in the temporal fossa is perforated by the zygomaticofacial nerve
It is perforated by the zygomaticotemporal nerve. (Last's p. 646)
Zygomaticus minor arises from the zygomaticomaxillary suture
Zygomaticus major arises from the surface of the zygomatic bone. (Last's p. 647)
Levator anguli oris arises from the incisive fossa

It arises from the canine fossa, lateral to the canine ridge.
The incisive slips of orbicularis oris arise near the midline. (Last's p. 647)
The supraorbital notch, infraorbital foramen and mental foramen lie in a vertical line
Last's notes this while the mandible is in position. (Last's p. 648)
The buccinator line on the maxilla runs close to the alveolar bone
It keeps well above the alveolar bone, from the first molar back to the tuberosity. (Last's p. 647)
The small inferior head of medial pterygoid arises from the maxillary tuberosity

It arises from the tuberosity and the pyramidal process of the palatine bone.
It overlaps the lower head of lateral pterygoid. (Last's p. 647)
The pterygomaxillary ligament runs from the tuberosity to the lateral pterygoid plate
It runs from the tuberosity to the tip of the hamulus, for buccinator. (Last's p. 647)
Buccinator and levator anguli oris attachments bisect the maxillary sinus
Its lower half lies deep to the vestibule, its upper half deep to the face. (Last's p. 648)
The frontal bone occupies the upper half of the anterior view of the skull
It occupies the upper third; maxillae and mandible the other two-thirds. (Last's p. 647)
Rectus capitis posterior minor attaches medial to rectus capitis posterior major
Both lie alongside the foramen magnum below the inferior nuchal line. (Last's p. 648)
The superior oblique attaches medially between the nuchal lines
Semispinalis capitis attaches medially, superior oblique laterally. (Last's p. 648)
The inferior nuchal line lies halfway between the superior nuchal line and foramen magnum
It is concentric with both. (Last's p. 648)
The external occipital crest runs from the protuberance to the mastoid process

It runs in the midline from the protuberance to the foramen magnum.
The superior nuchal line runs to the mastoid. (Last's p. 648)

questions.s: Last's survey of the skull base:
o: One-third of the foramen magnum lies in front of the line joining the mastoid tips
Two-thirds of each condyle lies in front of the line. (Last's p. 648)
The back of the nose is twice the width of the foramen magnum
It is the same width as the diameter of the foramen magnum. (Last's p. 648)
The mastoid–pterygoid line is divided into thirds by the styloid process and spine of the sphenoid
This locates the stylomastoid foramen and foramen spinosum. (Last's p. 648)
The pharyngeal tubercle lies two-thirds of the way from foramen magnum to vomer
It lies one-third of the way. (Last's p. 648)
Its transverse diameter is rather less than one-third of the intermastoid distance
It is oval with the long diameter anteroposterior. (Last's p. 648)
The meningeal branches of the vertebral artery lie inside the fibrous dura

They lie outside the dura, between it and the periosteum.
So do veins from the occipital sinuses. (Last's p. 649)
The alar ligaments attach medial to the anterior pole of each condyle
Each attaches to a triangular area limited in front by a ridge joining the condylar anterior poles. (Last's p. 649)
The posterior atlanto-occipital membrane attaches to less than half the foramen margin
It attaches to a curve of more than half the foramen. (Last's p. 649)
The atlanto-occipital joint permits some abduction but no rotation
The egg-shaped convexity allows nodding and some abduction. (Last's p. 649)
The condylar canal carries a vein from the transverse sinus
It carries a vein from the bottom of the sigmoid sinus to the suboccipital plexus. (Last's p. 649)
The hypoglossal canal lies deep to the summit of the condyle

It is at the site of the original epiphysis.
XII emerges medial to the jugular foramen. (Last's p. 649)
The occipital artery grooves the suture between jugular process and petrous bone
It grooves the suture between the jugular process and the mastoid. (Last's p. 649)
Rectus capitis anterior lies behind longus capitis on the basiocciput
It lies immediately in front of the occipital condyle and medial to the hypoglossal canal. (Last's p. 649)
The jugular process gives attachment to rectus capitis anterior

It gives attachment to rectus capitis lateralis.
The prevertebral fascia attaches behind the IJV. (Last's p. 649)
The mucous membrane of the nasopharynx is attached to the periosteum of the basiocciput
In front of the pharyngeal tubercle the bone roofs the nasopharynx. (Last's p. 649)
The basiocciput fuses with the basisphenoid at 15 years
It fuses at 25 years. (Last's p. 649)
Styloglossus arises low down on the front of the styloid process
Stylopharyngeus arises high medially, stylohyoid high posteriorly. (Last's p. 649-50)
The stylomastoid foramen lies in front of the styloid base
It lies behind the base of the styloid process. (Last's p. 650)
The stylomastoid foramen transmits a branch of the posterior auricular artery
It transmits the facial nerve and the stylomastoid branch. (Last's p. 650)
Last's says the stylomandibular ligament runs from the styloid tip
It is a thickening of parotid fascia from the vaginal process; Last's suggests "vaginomandibular" would be clearer. (Last's p. 650)
The cochlear canaliculus opens in the floor of the glossopharyngeal notch
IX's ganglia lie in the notch. (Last's p. 650)
The tympanic branch of IX passes through the carotid canal
It passes through a foramen in the centre of the ridge between jugular notch and carotid canal. (Last's p. 650)
Levator palati arises from the apex of the petrous bone and the cartilaginous tube
The pharyngobasilar fascia is attached behind it. (Last's p. 650)
The internal carotid artery passes through the foramen lacerum

Apart from minute emissary veins no major structure passes through it.
It is closed by dense fibrous tissue. (Last's p. 650)
The auricular branch of the vagus emerges between the tympanic part and mastoid
Last's calls it trespassing, emerging from imprisonment between the bones. (Last's p. 650)
The suprameatal spine belongs to the tympanic part
It is on the squamous bone, completing the bony ring of the meatus. (Last's p. 650)
The mastoid antrum lies 15 mm deep to the suprameatal triangle
The triangle is enclosed by tangents to the meatus and the suprameatal spine. (Last's p. 650)
The cartilaginous auditory tube runs parallel with the skull base
It passes down to the nasopharynx at about 20°. (Last's p. 650)
The tegmen tympani flange divides the squamotympanic fissure medially
It splits it into the petrosquamous fissure in front and the petrotympanic fissure behind. (Last's p. 651)
The jaw capsule attaches to the petrotympanic fissure

The capsule attaches to the petrosquamous fissure in front.
The chorda tympani emerges from the petrotympanic fissure. (Last's p. 651)
The tegmen flange forms the lateral boundary of the bony auditory tube
It encloses the canal for tensor tympani. (Last's p. 651)
The mandibular fossa lies exactly transversely
Its lateral end lies a little farther forward than its medial end, matching the condyle. (Last's p. 651)
The sphenomandibular ligament attaches to the tip of the spine of the sphenoid
The base of the spine is perforated by the foramen spinosum. (Last's p. 651)
The foramen of Vesalius lies lateral to the foramen ovale
It lies medial to it, for a vein from cavernous sinus to pterygoid plexus. (Last's p. 651)
A petrosal foramen, when present, lies behind the foramen ovale

It transmits the lesser petrosal nerve.
Without it the nerve uses the foramen ovale. (Last's p. 651)
The lower head of lateral pterygoid arises from the infratemporal surface of the greater wing
The upper head arises there; the lower head arises from the lateral surface of the lateral plate. (Last's p. 651-2)
The pterygomandibular raphe is attached to the tip of the hamulus
So is the pterygomaxillary ligament, which converts the hamulus into a canal for tensor palati. (Last's p. 652)
The upper head of medial pterygoid arises from the lateral surface of the lateral plate
It arises from the medial surface of the lateral plate. (Last's p. 652)
The lateral pterygoid plate is attached to the skull at the anterior pole of the foramen ovale
It springs from a common stem with the medial plate. (Last's p. 652)
The pterygoid notch is filled by the maxillary tuberosity
It is filled by the pyramidal process of the palatine bone. (Last's p. 652)

questions.s: Concerning canals in the roof of the nose (Last's):
o: The vomerovaginal canal carries the pharyngeal branch of the sphenopalatine artery
It lies between the vaginal process and the vomer. (Last's p. 652)
The palatovaginal canal opens in the nasal vault 2 cm in front of its posterior limit

It opens half a centimetre in front.
It carries the pharyngeal nerve and pharyngeal branch of the maxillary artery. (Last's p. 652)
The posterior opening of the pterygoid canal is in line with the medial pterygoid plate
Last's notes this on the disarticulated sphenoid. (Last's p. 652)
The hard palate is arched mainly by upward concavity of the palatal processes
It is arched more by the downward projecting alveolar processes. (Last's p. 652)
The floor of the middle fossa is level with the upper border of the zygomatic arch
The anterior fossa floor is level with the upper orbital margin. (Last's p. 653)
Internal skull sutures are more tortuous than external ones
They are much less tortuous and ossify sooner. (Last's p. 653)
The optic canal lies in the middle cranial fossa
So does the prechiasmatic groove; its anterior margin divides anterior and middle fossae centrally. (Last's p. 653)
The jugum of the sphenoid is part of the lesser wing

It is part of the body, joining the lesser wings.
It articulates with the cribriform plate. (Last's p. 653)
The anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery is often tunnelled at the pterion
It runs up and back through bone for a short distance. (Last's p. 653)
The foramen caecum transmits a constant vein in adults
It is plugged by falx fibrous tissue, making a huge Sharpey's fibre. (Last's p. 653)
Last's calls the slit beside the crista galli the "nasal slit"

It transmits the anterior ethmoidal nerve and vessels into the roof of the nose.
It has no official name. (Last's p. 653)
The orbital part of the frontal bone is concave over the orbit
It is convex and ridged in roughly H-shape. (Last's p. 653)
The middle clinoid process lies at the lateral end of the tuberculum sellae
It is medial to the carotid groove. (Last's p. 653)
The diaphragma sellae extends only to the anterior clinoid processes

It sweeps from the tuberculum sellae to the anterior and posterior clinoid processes.
It roofs the fossa and cavernous sinuses. (Last's p. 653)
The optic chiasma lies at a higher level well behind the prechiasmatic groove
Above the groove lie the anterior communicating artery and the rostrum. (Last's p. 654)
The posterior clinoid processes belong to the lesser wing
They are on the dorsum sellae; the anterior clinoids belong to the lesser wing. (Last's p. 653)

questions.s: Concerning the petrous apex and floor (Last's):
o: The petroclinoid ligament runs from the apical spike halfway up the dorsum sellae
Medial to the spike is a groove for the inferior petrosal sinus and VI. (Last's p. 654)
The arcuate eminence is made by the lateral semicircular canal
It is made by the anterior semicircular canal. (Last's p. 654)
The lesser petrosal groove runs towards the foramen ovale
It is parallel and anterolateral to the greater petrosal groove. (Last's p. 654)
The grooves on the vault are made by the middle meningeal arteries
Last's says they are made by the middle meningeal veins (actually dural sinuses). (Last's p. 654)

questions.s: Concerning foramina of the middle fossa (Last's):
o: The nervus spinosus commonly runs with the accessory meningeal artery
It commonly passes through the foramen ovale rather than the foramen spinosum. (Last's p. 654)
The lateral wall of the cavernous sinus blends with periosteum at the medial margin of foramen rotundum
It blends at the lateral margin. (Last's p. 654)
The superior orbital fissure is closed by dura lateral to the line of the foramen rotundum
Medially it is open for the cavernous sinus and its nerves. (Last's p. 654)
The lingula of the sphenoid lies medial to the carotid groove
It is the prominent lateral ridge of the groove; the pterygoid canal opens beneath it. (Last's p. 654)

questions.s: Concerning the middle and posterior fossae (Last's):
o: The sphenoparietal sinus enters the roof of the cavernous sinus at the anterior clinoid
It runs below the margin of the lesser wing from the pterion. (Last's p. 655)
The narrower transverse groove usually receives the superior sagittal sinus
The sagittal groove usually turns right into the wider groove; the narrower (usually left) begins with the straight sinus. (Last's p. 655)
The larger jugular foramen is almost always on the side receiving the superior sagittal sinus
This is more commonly the right. (Last's p. 655)
The internal occipital protuberance lies above the external one
It lies opposite the external occipital protuberance. (Last's p. 655)

questions.s: Concerning the clivus and jugular tubercle (Last's):
o: The jugular tubercle is the line of fusion of basiocciput and lateral occipital part
It lies above the occipital condyle, with the hypoglossal canal between. (Last's p. 655)
The medulla lies above the jugular tubercles on the clivus
The medulla lies between the tubercles; above them the clivus broadens to lodge the pons. (Last's p. 655)
The groove behind the jugular tubercle lodges IX, X and XI
They run in it to the jugular foramen. (Last's p. 655)
The hypoglossal canal runs vertically through the bone
It perforates the bone obliquely, almost transversely. (Last's p. 655)
In the anterior fossa only the ethmoid ossifies in cartilage
The floors of the middle and posterior fossae ossify in cartilage. (Last's p. 655)
The sphenoid pterygoid plates ossify in cartilage

They ossify in membrane, with the rest of the greater wing.
The body, lesser wing and base of the greater wing are cartilage. (Last's p. 657)
Fusion of jugular parts with the basiocciput coincides with eruption of the permanent dentition
At 6 years; squamous–jugular fusion (2 years) coincides with completion of milk teeth. (Last's p. 658)
The squamous–jugular occipital junction forms an anterior tangent to the foramen magnum
It forms a posterior tangent to the foramen magnum. (Last's p. 658)

questions.s: Concerning the disarticulated frontal and sphenoid (Last's):
o: The trochlear mark lies below the floor of the frontal sinus
Last's notes this on the frontal bone seen from below. (Last's p. 656)
The foramen caecum perforates the bone in most skulls
It is a blind pit; only in 1% does it perforate. (Last's p. 656)
The septum between the sphenoidal sinuses is always deviated
It is a backward projection of the rostrum. (Last's p. 657)
In the temporal fossa the greater wing overlaps the squamous temporal
In the temporal fossa the squamous overlaps the greater wing; in the infratemporal fossa the greater wing overlies the squamous. (Last's p. 657)

questions.s: Concerning the disarticulated temporal and occipital bones (Last's):
o: The carotid canal opens well to the lateral side of the petrous apex
Its exit is in the foramen lacerum after a right-angle bend. (Last's p. 657)
The aqueduct of the vestibule opens in front of the internal acoustic meatus
It opens behind the meatus, under a curtain-like flange of bone. (Last's p. 658)
The condylar canal passes back above the occipital condyle
It leaves the sigmoid groove on the jugular process. (Last's p. 658)
The frontal articulation with the greater wing stops short of the superior orbital fissure
It extends medially to bridge the fissure between greater and lesser wings. (Last's p. 657)

questions.s: Concerning the parietal and ethmoid bones (Last's):
o: The anterior middle meningeal groove runs just behind the anterior border of the parietal bone

Posterior division grooves run up and back.
This helps tell right from left. (Last's p. 659)
The ethmoid labyrinth has its own bony roof
It has no roof; it is overlapped by the orbital part of the frontal bone. (Last's p. 659)
Last's regards the infundibulum as a specialised anterior ethmoidal air cell
Its mucosa forms the frontonasal duct to the middle meatus. (Last's p. 659)
The posterior ethmoidal cells open on the bulla
Middle cells open on the bulla; posterior cells open below the superior concha. (Last's p. 659)
The anterior deficiency of the labyrinth is completed by the lacrimal bone
The posterior deficiency is completed by the sphenoidal concha and orbital process of the palatine. (Last's p. 659)
The superior concha is larger than the middle concha

The middle concha is the larger of the two.
They spring from a common stem. (Last's p. 659)
The uncinate process articulates with the inferior concha
It curves down in front of the bulla across the maxillary hiatus. (Last's p. 659)
The perpendicular plate articulates inferiorly with the vomer
Inferiorly it meets the septal cartilage; posteriorly the vomer and sphenoidal rostrum. (Last's p. 659)
The floor of a large maxillary sinus lies lower than the palatine process
It dips into the alveolar process. (Last's p. 660)
The lacrimal groove is directed down and somewhat forwards

It is directed down and somewhat back.
It makes a convexity on the medial sinus wall in front of the hiatus. (Last's p. 660)
Last's says greater palatine arteries run up through the incisive canal to the septum
The canal also transmits the nasopalatine nerves. (Last's p. 660)
The maxillary primary centre appears below the canine fossa at the eighth week
It appears above the canine fossa at the sixth week; the premaxilla a week later. (Last's p. 660)
The pyramidal process prevents the pterygoid plates from articulating with the maxilla
An uncritical glance might suggest they articulate, but the process intervenes. (Last's p. 661)
The upper head of palatopharyngeus arises in front of the palatine crest

It arises from the smooth area between the crest and the posterior border.
It contributes to Passavant's ridge. (Last's p. 661)
The palatine bone ossifies from a centre in the pyramidal process
It appears at the seventh week and spreads over the nasal capsule. (Last's p. 662)
The orbital process of the palatine bone forms the apex of the medial orbital wall

It forms a triangular apex to the floor of the orbit.
It is often excavated by a posterior ethmoidal cell. (Last's p. 662)
Its roof is the body of the sphenoid
Medial wall: perpendicular plate of palatine; anterior: maxilla; posterior: pterygoid root and greater wing. (Last's p. 662)
The sphenopalatine foramen lies in front of the anterior end of the middle concha
It lies immediately behind the posterior end of the middle concha. (Last's p. 662)
The sphenopalatine foramen is closed in life by nasal mucous membrane
It transmits the posterior superior nasal and nasopalatine nerves and the sphenopalatine artery. (Last's p. 662)
The ethmoidal crest of the palatine bone articulates with the inferior concha
The conchal crest (halfway up) is for the inferior concha; the ethmoidal crest is for the middle concha. (Last's p. 662)
The zygomatic bone ossifies from three centres that fuse at midterm
Failure gives two or three parts, very often two in the Japanese. (Last's p. 662)
The inferior border of the nasal bone articulates with the alar cartilage

In life it articulates with the lateral nasal cartilage.
It is notched by the external nasal nerve. (Last's p. 662)
The nasal bones articulate with the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid
They meet each other in the midline and the perpendicular plate. (Last's p. 662)
The lacrimal bone overlaps the posterior ethmoidal air cells
It overlaps the anterior ethmoidal air cells. (Last's p. 662)

questions.s: Concerning the lacrimal bone, inferior concha and vomer (Last's):
o: The inferior concha ossifies in the cartilage of the nasal capsule

Its centre appears at about mid-term.
Most facial bones ossify in membrane. (Last's p. 663)
The hamulus of the lacrimal bone projects from the upper end of the posterior lacrimal crest
It projects forwards from the lower end, articulating with the maxilla at the top of the nasolacrimal canal. (Last's p. 663)
The maxillary process of the inferior concha overlaps the lower part of the maxillary hiatus
It projects down from the middle of the upper border. (Last's p. 663)
The vomer ossifies from a single midline centre
A centre appears on either side of the cartilaginous septum at the eighth week, forming two plates. (Last's p. 663)

questions.s: Concerning the outer surface of the mandible (Last's):
o: Depressor anguli oris arises just below the mental foramen
Depressor labii inferioris arises in front of it. (Last's p. 663)
The mental foramen faces forwards and slightly downwards

It faces backwards and slightly upwards.
It usually lies between the two premolars. (Last's p. 663)
Masseter inserts on the body as far forward as the second molar
It inserts behind the external oblique ridge. (Last's p. 663)
Buccinator is attached along the external oblique ridge as far as the canine
It is attached as far as the anterior border of the first molar. (Last's p. 663)

questions.s: Concerning the inner surface of the mandible (Last's):
o: Mylohyoid extends from level with the posterior border of the last molar to the midline

It may leave no mark near the midline.
Its line divides mouth from neck. (Last's p. 664)
Geniohyoid arises from the upper mental spines
Genioglossus arises from the upper and geniohyoid from the lower spines. (Last's p. 664)
The lingula lies level with the occlusal surfaces of the teeth
It lies in front of the mandibular foramen, halfway between the borders of the ramus. (Last's p. 664)
The mylohyoid groove ends at the anterior end of the submandibular fossa
It dies out at the posterior end of the submandibular fossa. (Last's p. 664)
The suprameatal fibres of temporalis are the only retractors of the head of the mandible
They insert along the posterior border of the coronoid process. (Last's p. 665)
The internal oblique ridge is sharper than the external oblique ridge

The external is sharp; the internal is usually more rounded.
The internal is the landmark for inferior alveolar block. (Last's p. 665)
The two condyles lie on the arc of a circle crossing the front of the foramen magnum
The transverse crest of each is directed medially and slightly backwards. (Last's p. 665)
The articular surface of the condyle is covered by hyaline cartilage
It is covered by fibrocartilage identical with the disc. (Last's p. 665)
It lies at the level of C3
Its greater horn projects back as far as the angle of the mandible. (Last's p. 665)
The lesser horn always fuses with the body
It may remain permanently connected by fibrous tissue. (Last's p. 665)
The hyoid marks the junction of oropharynx and laryngopharynx
It is level with the lateral glossoepiglottic folds, bisecting the epiglottis. (Last's p. 665)
The thyrohyoid membrane attaches to the lower border of the hyoid body

It attaches to the sharp upper border and hangs down inside the curve.
A bursa lies behind the body. (Last's p. 665)

questions.s: Concerning the cavernous sinus and its tributaries (Last's):
o: The superficial middle cerebral vein pierces the roof of the cavernous sinus near the emerging internal carotid
It crosses the subarachnoid space to do so. (Last's p. 567)
The sphenoparietal sinus runs above the edge of the lesser wing of the sphenoid
It runs beneath the edge of the lesser wing, between the dural layers. (Last's p. 567)
The superior petrosal sinus leaves the bottom of the posterior wall of the cavernous sinus
It leaves the top; the inferior petrosal leaves beneath the petroclinoid ligament. (Last's p. 567)
The abducent nerve lies above the petroclinoid ligament
It lies beneath it, within or alongside the inferior petrosal sinus. (Last's p. 567)
The superior sagittal sinus usually turns to the left at the internal occipital protuberance
It usually turns right; the straight sinus usually turns left. (Last's p. 563)
The sigmoid sinus may connect with the suboccipital plexus through the posterior condylar foramen
When the foramen is present. (Last's p. 564)
The basilar sinuses connect the two superior petrosal sinuses
They connect the two inferior petrosal sinuses, on the clivus. (Last's p. 564)
Thrombophlebitis of mastoid veins draining to the sigmoid sinus may cause cerebellar abscess
(Last's p. 564)
Entering cerebral arteries lie loose in pial sheaths surrounded by a perivascular space containing CSF
The pia is invaginated by them. (Last's p. 559)
Arachnoid villi are most numerous in the superior sagittal sinus and its lateral blood lakes
They aggregate into granulations with age. (Last's p. 559)
The fused dural layers strip easily from the vault but only with difficulty from the base
(Last's p. 560)
The outer (endosteal) dural layer is prolonged down the vertebral canal
Only the inner layer forms the spinal dura; the outer layer never leaves bone. (Last's p. 560)

questions.s: Concerning the vessels and nerves of the dura (Last's):
o: The middle meningeal artery supplies the cortex beneath it
It supplies the bones of the vault, not the brain. (Last's p. 562)
There are two frontal diploic veins on each side
One frontal, two parietal and one occipital. (Last's p. 562)
The middle meningeal artery enters the skull through the foramen ovale
Through the foramen spinosum; the accessory meningeal uses the foramen ovale. (Last's p. 562)
Cervical spondylosis may cause deep orbital pain referred from the upper cervical dural supply
Last's suggests the cervical supply extends beyond the foramen magnum. (Last's p. 563)
The pituitary stalk slopes downwards and backwards to the diaphragma
It slopes downwards and forwards. (Last's p. 569)
The optic chiasma lies in front of the diaphragma sellae
It lies above and towards the back of the diaphragma. (Last's p. 569)
The pars nervosa and pars intermedia are often called together the anterior lobe
They are often termed the posterior lobe. (Last's p. 569)
The upper part of the pituitary stalk is hollow, continuous with the third ventricle
The infundibulum. (Last's p. 569)
The trochlear nerve enters the middle fossa just behind the oculomotor nerve
It pierces the back of the cavernous sinus roof. (Last's p. 570)
The labyrinthine artery divides in the internal acoustic meatus
Its branches accompany the nerves through the bony plate. (Last's p. 572)
IX, X and XI cross the occipital bone behind the jugular tubercle in that order
(Last's p. 572)
The vertebral artery gives two small posterior spinal arteries after piercing the dura
(Last's p. 573)
